claim: Human B cells secrete active ST6GAL1 sialyltransferase.
source: Human B cells secrete active ST6GAL1 sialyltransferase that remodels progenitor cell surface glycans to suppress granulopoiesis.
evidence: Demonstrated through western blot and enzymatic activity assays of conditioned medium from B lymphoblastoid cell lines (Figure 1c, 1d)

claim: ST6GAL1 from human B cells remodels progenitor cell surface glycans to suppress granulopoiesis.
source: Human B cells secrete active ST6GAL1 sialyltransferase that remodels progenitor cell surface glycans to suppress granulopoiesis.
evidence: Demonstrated through co-culture experiments showing increased SNA reactivity and decreased Gr-1 expression in HSPCs (Figure 3)

claim: ST6GAL1 from B cells alters the sialylation profile of bone marrow populations in mouse models.
source: In mouse models, ST6GAL1 from B cells alters the sialylation profile of bone marrow populations, and mature IgD+ B cells were enriched in sialylated bone marrow niches.
evidence: Demonstrated through bone marrow transplantation experiments showing increased SNA reactivity in various bone marrow cell populations (Figure 4)

claim: Mature IgD+ B cells are enriched in sialylated bone marrow niches.
source: In mouse models, ST6GAL1 from B cells alters the sialylation profile of bone marrow populations, and mature IgD+ B cells were enriched in sialylated bone marrow niches.
evidence: Demonstrated through immunofluorescence analysis showing positive correlation between IgD+ B cells and SNA reactivity in bone marrow regions (Figure 5)

claim: In clinical multiple myeloma, ST6GAL1 abundance in multiple myeloma cells negatively correlates with neutrophil abundance.
source: In clinical multiple myeloma, ST6GAL1 abundance in the multiple myeloma cells negatively correlated with neutrophil abundance.
evidence: Demonstrated through histological analysis of human bone marrow samples showing negative correlation (r2 = 0.42, p=0.0083) between ST6GAL1 score and segmented neutrophils (Figure 6)

claim: ST6GAL1 is a glycan-modifying enzyme that mediates the attachment of α2,6-sialic acids.
source: The sialyltransferase ST6GAL1 is a glycan-modifying enzyme mediating the attachment of α2,6-sialic acids.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ST6GAL1 function

claim: ST6GAL1 canonically resides within the intracellular ER-Golgi secretory apparatus.
source: Canonically, it resides within the intracellular ER-Golgi secretory apparatus, but there is also an extracellular blood-borne form (Kim et al., 1971; Bernacki and Kim, 1977; Ip, 1980).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: There is an extracellular blood-borne form of ST6GAL1.
source: Canonically, it resides within the intracellular ER-Golgi secretory apparatus, but there is also an extracellular blood-borne form (Kim et al., 1971; Bernacki and Kim, 1977; Ip, 1980).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: A number of other terminal glycosyltransferases are present in systemic circulation in addition to ST6GAL1.
source: In addition to ST6GAL1, a number of other terminal glycosyltransferases are also present in systemic circulation (Lee-Sundlov et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: High levels of blood ST6GAL1 have been associated with poor patient outcomes in metastatic cancers.
source: Fluctuating levels of blood-borne ST6GAL1 are associated with a wide array of conditions, especially metastatic cancers, where high levels of blood enzyme have been associated with poor patient outcomes (Ip and Dao, 1978; Evans et al., 1980; Weiser et al., 1981; Berge et al., 1982; Dao et al., 1986; Cohen et al., 1989a; Magalhães et al., 2017; Rodrigues et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior literature

claim: Elevated blood ST6GAL1 has been associated with systemic inflammation.
source: Early reports also associated elevated blood ST6GAL1 with systemic inflammation (Kaplan et al., 1983; Jamieson et al., 1993), atherosclerosis (Gracheva et al., 1999), Alzheimer's disease (Maguire et al., 1994), and alcohol-induced liver disease (Malagolini et al., 1989; Garige et al., 2006; Gong et al., 2007; Gong et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Elevated blood ST6GAL1 has been associated with atherosclerosis.
source: Early reports also associated elevated blood ST6GAL1 with systemic inflammation (Kaplan et al., 1983; Jamieson et al., 1993), atherosclerosis (Gracheva et al., 1999), Alzheimer's disease (Maguire et al., 1994), and alcohol-induced liver disease (Malagolini et al., 1989; Garige et al., 2006; Gong et al., 2007; Gong et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Elevated blood ST6GAL1 has been associated with Alzheimer's disease.
source: Early reports also associated elevated blood ST6GAL1 with systemic inflammation (Kaplan et al., 1983; Jamieson et al., 1993), atherosclerosis (Gracheva et al., 1999), Alzheimer's disease (Maguire et al., 1994), and alcohol-induced liver disease (Malagolini et al., 1989; Garige et al., 2006; Gong et al., 2007; Gong et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Elevated blood ST6GAL1 has been associated with alcohol-induced liver disease.
source: Early reports also associated elevated blood ST6GAL1 with systemic inflammation (Kaplan et al., 1983; Jamieson et al., 1993), atherosclerosis (Gracheva et al., 1999), Alzheimer's disease (Maguire et al., 1994), and alcohol-induced liver disease (Malagolini et al., 1989; Garige et al., 2006; Gong et al., 2007; Gong et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Blood-borne ST6GAL1 can profoundly modify leukocyte differentiation by attenuating G-CSF dependent granulocyte production.
source: Previously, we observed that blood-borne ST6GAL1 can profoundly modify leukocyte differentiation by attenuating G-CSF dependent granulocyte production (Dougher et al., 2017) while promoting BAFF-dependent survival in B cells (Irons and Lau, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors

claim: Blood-borne ST6GAL1 promotes BAFF-dependent survival in B cells.
source: Previously, we observed that blood-borne ST6GAL1 can profoundly modify leukocyte differentiation by attenuating G-CSF dependent granulocyte production (Dougher et al., 2017) while promoting BAFF-dependent survival in B cells (Irons and Lau, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors

claim: Circulatory ST6GAL1 insufficiency results in an exuberant granulocytic inflammatory response in mouse models.
source: In mouse models, circulatory ST6GAL1 insufficiency results in an exuberant granulocytic inflammatory response (Nasirikenari et al., 2010; Nasirikenari et al., 2006) that can be therapeutically ameliorated by intravenous infusion of recombinant ST6GAL1 (Nasirikenari et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Exuberant granulocytic inflammatory response due to ST6GAL1 insufficiency can be therapeutically ameliorated by intravenous infusion of recombinant ST6GAL1.
source: In mouse models, circulatory ST6GAL1 insufficiency results in an exuberant granulocytic inflammatory response (Nasirikenari et al., 2010; Nasirikenari et al., 2006) that can be therapeutically ameliorated by intravenous infusion of recombinant ST6GAL1 (Nasirikenari et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Extracellular, liver-derived ST6GAL1 is a major determinant of serum immunoglobulin G sialylation.
source: Extracellular, liver-derived ST6GAL1 is also a major determinant of serum immunoglobulin G sialylation, which activates anti-inflammatory pathways within innate immune cells through Fc receptors (Jones et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2012; Pagan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Serum immunoglobulin G sialylation activates anti-inflammatory pathways within innate immune cells through Fc receptors.
source: Extracellular, liver-derived ST6GAL1 is also a major determinant of serum immunoglobulin G sialylation, which activates anti-inflammatory pathways within innate immune cells through Fc receptors (Jones et al., 2016; Jones et al., 2012; Pagan et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Activated platelets can supply the necessary sugar donor-substrate to support extrinsic glycosylation reactions in the periphery.
source: In the periphery, activated platelets can supply the necessary sugar donor-substrate to support such extrinsic glycosylation reactions (Lee-Sundlov et al., 2017; Manhardt et al., 2017; Wandall et al., 2012; Lee et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The principal source of extracellular ST6GAL1 in circulation is believed to be the liver.
source: The principal source of extracellular ST6GAL1 in circulation is believed to be the liver (Jamieson et al., 1993; Appenheimer et al., 2003; Lammers and Jamieson, 1986), where ST6GAL1 expression is activated by glucocorticoids and IL-6 (Jamieson et al., 1993; Jamieson et al., 1987; Wang et al., 1990; Dalziel et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: ST6GAL1 expression in the liver is activated by glucocorticoids and IL-6.
source: The principal source of extracellular ST6GAL1 in circulation is believed to be the liver (Jamieson et al., 1993; Appenheimer et al., 2003; Lammers and Jamieson, 1986), where ST6GAL1 expression is activated by glucocorticoids and IL-6 (Jamieson et al., 1993; Jamieson et al., 1987; Wang et al., 1990; Dalziel et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: B cells robustly express ST6GAL1.
source: However, B cells also robustly express ST6GAL1, which synthesizes the ligands for sialic acid-binding receptors CD22 and Siglec-G (Wuensch et al., 2000; Müller and Nitschke, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: ST6GAL1 synthesizes the ligands for sialic acid-binding receptors CD22 and Siglec-G.
source: However, B cells also robustly express ST6GAL1, which synthesizes the ligands for sialic acid-binding receptors CD22 and Siglec-G (Wuensch et al., 2000; Müller and Nitschke, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: B cells secrete functionally active ST6GAL1 that sialylates hematopoietic progenitors in co-culture to suppress granulopoietic differentiation.
source: B cells secrete functionally active ST6GAL1 that sialylates hematopoietic progenitors in co-culture to suppress granulopoietic differentiation.
evidence: Demonstrated through co-culture experiments showing increased SNA reactivity and decreased Gr-1 expression (Figure 3)

claim: There is a positive correlation between IgD+ B cells and richly α2,6-sialylated niches of the bone marrow in mouse models.
source: In mouse models, we observed a positive correlation between IgD+ B cells and richly α2,6-sialylated niches of the bone marrow.
evidence: Demonstrated through immunofluorescence analysis showing correlation (R2 = 0.2448, p<0.05) between IgD+ B cells and SNA reactivity (Figure 5)

claim: In bone marrow specimens of treatment-naïve human multiple myeloma, there is a striking negative association between marrow plasma cell ST6GAL1 expression and the prevalence of bone marrow neutrophils.
source: In bone marrow specimens of treatment-naïve human multiple myeloma, there was a striking negative association between marrow plasma cell ST6GAL1 expression and the prevalence of bone marrow neutrophils.
evidence: Demonstrated through histological analysis showing negative correlation (r2 = 0.42, p=0.0083) (Figure 6)

claim: This study is the first to demonstrate that the liver is not the sole source of ST6GAL1 responsible for extracellular sialylation.
source: Our study is the first to demonstrate that the liver is not the sole source of ST6GAL1 responsible for extracellular sialylation, and underscores a novel potential relationship between B lymphocytes and hematopoietic progenitors influencing neutrophil production in the marrow.
evidence: Demonstrated through bone marrow transplantation experiments showing hematopoietic cells can restore blood ST6GAL1 (Figure 4)

claim: B cell expression of ST6GAL1 is critical for B cell development and function secondary to engagement of the lineage-specific lectin CD22 with α2,6-sialic acid.
source: B cell expression of ST6GAL1 is critical for B cell development and function secondary to engagement of the lineage-specific lectin CD22 with α2,6-sialic acid (Hennet et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: A hepatocyte conditional knockout of St6gal1 results in vastly reduced serum α2,6-sialyltransferase activity.
source: Although ST6GAL1 is expressed in multiple tissue and cell types, it is thought that secreted, extracellular ST6GAL1 is exclusively derived from the liver, as a hepatocyte conditional knockout of St6gal1 results in vastly reduced serum α2,6-sialyltransferase activity (Appenheimer et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Maximal ST6GAL1 expression in mouse bone marrow and splenic B cell populations occurs in early transitional and mature stages of development.
source: We have recently analyzed the expression of ST6GAL1 within bone marrow and splenic B cell populations in mice and found that maximal ST6GAL1 expression occurred in early transitional and mature stages of development (Irons and Lau, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors

claim: ST6GAL1 mRNA expression was detectable in all B lymphoblastoid cell lines except myeloma line RPMI 8226.
source: ST6GAL1 mRNA expression was detectable in all cell lines except myeloma line RPMI 8226, with highest expression observed in the Burkitt lymphoma line Louckes (Figure 1a).
evidence: Demonstrated through RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 1a

claim: Highest ST6GAL1 mRNA expression among B lymphoblastoid cell lines was observed in the Burkitt lymphoma line Louckes.
source: ST6GAL1 mRNA expression was detectable in all cell lines except myeloma line RPMI 8226, with highest expression observed in the Burkitt lymphoma line Louckes (Figure 1a).
evidence: Demonstrated through RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 1a

claim: Louckes is a germinal center B cell derivative.
source: Since Louckes is a germinal center B cell derivative, this observation is consistent with our previous observations that BCR activation induces ST6GAL1 expression (Wang et al., 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Louckes cell line

claim: BCR activation induces ST6GAL1 expression.
source: Since Louckes is a germinal center B cell derivative, this observation is consistent with our previous observations that BCR activation induces ST6GAL1 expression (Wang et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work by the authors

claim: BACE1 expression was detected within all B lymphoblastoid cell lines except the myeloma cell MM1.S.
source: Expression of the β-site amyloid precursor protein-cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE1), thought to be required to liberate ST6GAL1 from its N-terminal membrane anchor prior to secretion (Kitazume et al., 2001; Deng et al., 2017), was detected within all lines except the myeloma cell MM1.S (Figure 1a).
evidence: Demonstrated through RT-qPCR analysis shown in Figure 1a

claim: BACE1 is thought to be required to liberate ST6GAL1 from its N-terminal membrane anchor prior to secretion.
source: Expression of the β-site amyloid precursor protein-cleaving enzyme 1 (BACE1), thought to be required to liberate ST6GAL1 from its N-terminal membrane anchor prior to secretion (Kitazume et al., 2001; Deng et al., 2017), was detected within all lines except the myeloma cell MM1.S (Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: All B lymphoblastoid cells examined expressed the cellular full-length ST6GAL1 form of 50 kDa.
source: All cells examined expressed, as expected, the cellular full-length ST6GAL1 form of 50 kDa. (Figure 1b).
evidence: Demonstrated through western blot analysis shown in Figure 1b

claim: All B lymphoblastoid cell lines except RPMI-8226 released measurable ST6GAL1 protein in a time-dependent manner into the medium.
source: All cell lines, except RPMI-8226, released measurable ST6GAL1 protein in a time-dependent manner into the medium (Figure 1c).
evidence: Demonstrated through western blot analysis of conditioned medium shown in Figure 1c

claim: B cells (NALM-6, Louckes) expressing BACE1 secreted the expected 42 kDa soluble form of ST6GAL1.
source: B cells (NALM-6, Louckes) expressing BACE1 secreted the expected 42 kDa soluble form of ST6GAL1, consistent with the proteolytic liberation of the soluble catalytic active domain from the full-length protein by BACE1.
evidence: Demonstrated through western blot analysis of conditioned medium (Figure 1c)

claim: The 42 kDa soluble form of ST6GAL1 is consistent with the proteolytic liberation of the soluble catalytic active domain from the full-length protein by BACE1.
source: B cells (NALM-6, Louckes) expressing BACE1 secreted the expected 42 kDa soluble form of ST6GAL1, consistent with the proteolytic liberation of the soluble catalytic active domain from the full-length protein by BACE1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of BACE1 and the observed molecular weight

claim: MM1.S cells, which do not express BACE1, released predominately the 50 kDa form of ST6GAL1.
source: MM1.S cells, which do not express BACE1, released predominately the 50 kDa form.
evidence: Demonstrated through western blot analysis of conditioned medium (Figure 1c)

claim: The release of unprocessed, full-length ST6GAL1 has never been reported before this study.
source: To the best of our knowledge, the release of unprocessed, full-length ST6GAL1 has never been reported.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the finding based on literature review

claim: All released ST6GAL1 from B lymphoblastoid cell lines was catalytically active, regardless of the larger size observed particularly in MM1.S.
source: Enzymatic assay confirmed that all released ST6GAL1 was catalytically active, regardless of the larger size observed particularly in MM1.S (Figure 1d).
evidence: Demonstrated through sialyltransferase activity assay shown in Figure 1d

claim: Louckes conditioned media alone was insufficient to restore HepG2 cell surface SNA reactivity.
source: Louckes conditioned media alone was insufficient to restore HepG2 cell surface SNA reactivity, but required the presence of the sugar donor substrate, CMP-Sia.
evidence: Demonstrated through immunofluorescence and flow cytometry experiments (Figure 2)

claim: Louckes conditioned media required the presence of the sugar donor substrate CMP-Sia to restore HepG2 cell surface SNA reactivity.
source: Louckes conditioned media alone was insufficient to restore HepG2 cell surface SNA reactivity, but required the presence of the sugar donor substrate, CMP-Sia.
evidence: Demonstrated through immunofluorescence and flow cytometry experiments (Figure 2)

claim: The sialyltransferase secreted by B cells is enzymatically active and capable of extrinsic sialylation of cell surface glycans when supplemented with the sugar donor.
source: These results indicate that the sialyltransferase secreted by B cells is enzymatically active and capable of extrinsic sialylation of cell surface glycans when supplemented with the sugar donor.
evidence: Demonstrated through experiments showing restoration of SNA reactivity on HepG2 cells (Figure 2)

claim: Mice deficient in circulatory ST6GAL1 have exaggerated neutrophilia inducible by various inflammatory stimuli.
source: Mice deficient in circulatory ST6GAL1 have exaggerated neutrophilia inducible by various inflammatory stimuli (Nasirikenari et al., 2010; Nasirikenari et al., 2006; Appenheimer et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Supplementation of recombinant ST6GAL1 is sufficient to blunt development of G-CSF and IL-5 dependent granulocytic colonies from whole bone marrow cells in vitro.
source: Supplementation of recombinant ST6GAL1 is sufficient to blunt development of G-CSF and IL-5 dependent granulocytic colonies from whole bone marrow cells in vitro (Jones et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Elevation of blood ST6GAL1 reduces bone marrow neutrophil abundance and neutrophilic inflammation secondary to sialylation of the multipotent granulocyte/monocyte progenitor (GMP).
source: In vivo, elevation of blood ST6GAL1 reduces bone marrow neutrophil abundance and neutrophilic inflammation secondary to sialylation of the multipotent granulocyte/monocyte progenitor (GMP).
evidence: This is a summary statement based on prior work

claim: Ex vivo sialylation of GMPs potently inhibits G-CSF induced STAT3 signaling to reduce expression of myeloperoxidase, C/EBP-α, Gr-1, and ultimately, neutrophil production.
source: Ex vivo sialylation of GMPs potently inhibits G-CSF induced STAT3 signaling to reduce expression of myeloperoxidase, C/EBP-α, Gr-1, and ultimately, neutrophil production (Dougher et al., 2017).

claim: Early B cells, mature B cells, and antibody-producing plasma cells represent a significant fraction of bone marrow cells.
source: Early B cells, mature B cells, and antibody-producing plasma cells represent a significant fraction of bone marrow cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about bone marrow composition

claim: Co-culture of HSPC with ST6GAL1 secreting B cell lines (NALM-6, Louckes, and MM1.S) increased cell-surface SNA reactivity of HSPC in a dose-dependent manner.
source: The ST6GAL1 secreting B cell lines, NALM-6, Louckes, and MM1.S, increased cell-surface SNA reactivity of HSPC in a dose-dependent manner.

claim: RPMI-8226 cells, which do not release ST6GAL1, did not raise SNA reactivity on the co-cultured HSPCs.
source: RPMI-8226 cells, which do not release ST6GAL1, did not raise SNA reactivity on the co-cultured HSPCs.
evidence: Demonstrated through flow cytometry analysis of co-cultures (Figure 3b)

claim: Cell surface MAL-II reactivity had no apparent correlation with ST6GAL1 status in the co-cultured B cells.
source: In contrast, cell surface MAL-II reactivity had no apparent correlation with ST6GAL1 status in the co-cultured B cells.

claim: Co-cultured murine HSPCs exhibited a significant negative correlation between Gr-1 expression and increasing cell surface SNA reactivity (r2 = 0.66, p<0.0001).
source: Co-cultured murine HSPCs exhibited a significant negative correlation between Gr-1 expression and increasing cell surface SNA reactivity (r2 = 0.66, p<0.0001) (Figure 3d).

claim: A similar correlation was not observed between pan-myeloid marker CD11b and SNA reactivity.
source: A similar correlation was not observed between pan-myeloid marker CD11b and SNA reactivity (Figure 3d), suggesting a specific effect on granulocytes, in contrast to total myeloid cells.

claim: The presence of ST6GAL1 has a specific effect on granulocytes, in contrast to total myeloid cells.
source: A similar correlation was not observed between pan-myeloid marker CD11b and SNA reactivity (Figure 3d), suggesting a specific effect on granulocytes, in contrast to total myeloid cells.

claim: There was a significant, dose-dependent increase in CD11b-/Gr-1- undifferentiated population in co-cultures with ST6GAL1 expressing B cell lines.
source: Consistently, there was a significant, dose-dependent increase in this undifferentiated population in co-cultures with ST6GAL1 expressing B cell lines, suggesting that the presence of ST6GAL1 is correlated with maintenance of a less differentiated state.

claim: The presence of ST6GAL1 is correlated with maintenance of a less differentiated state in HSPCs.
source: Consistently, there was a significant, dose-dependent increase in this undifferentiated population in co-cultures with ST6GAL1 expressing B cell lines, suggesting that the presence of ST6GAL1 is correlated with maintenance of a less differentiated state.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed increase in undifferentiated cells

claim: Neither the Ly6C or Ly6G epitope of Gr-1 is predicted to contain any N-linked glycans.
source: Since neither the Ly6C or Ly6G epitope of Gr-1 is predicted to contain any N-linked glycans, this relationship is unlikely a direct result of altered antibody binding due to epitope sialylation.
evidence: This is based on structural knowledge of the Gr-1 epitopes

claim: The relationship between ST6GAL1 and Gr-1 expression is unlikely a direct result of altered antibody binding due to epitope sialylation.
source: Since neither the Ly6C or Ly6G epitope of Gr-1 is predicted to contain any N-linked glycans, this relationship is unlikely a direct result of altered antibody binding due to epitope sialylation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of N-linked glycans on Gr-1 epitopes

claim: ST6GAL1 deletion in MM1.S cells abrogated the dose-dependent increase in SNA reactivity on murine HSPCs.
source: In co-cultures with murine St6gal1KO HSPC, ST6GAL1 deletion in MM1.S cells abrogated the dose-dependent increase in SNA reactivity on murine HSPCs (Figure 3f, left).

claim: Loss of ST6GAL1 in MM1.S cells attenuated the dose-dependent suppression of Gr-1 expression by co-cultured MM1.S cells.

claim: Blood α2,3-sialyltransferase activity remained within the limits of resting WT animals in bone marrow chimeras.
source: Blood α2,3-sialyltransferase activity, which did not depend on ST6GAL1, was unchanged and remained within the limits of resting WT (native C57BL/6) animals (Figure 4b).

claim: Blood accumulation of α2,6-sialyltransferase activity was dependent on re-establishment of ST6GAL1-competent hematopoietic cells.
source: In contrast, blood accumulation of α2,6-sialyltransferase activity against Gal(β4)GlcNAc-o-Bn acceptor was dependent on re-establishment of ST6GAL1-competent hematopoietic cells, and increased and even surpassed the baseline for resting WT mice by week 8 (Figure 4c).

claim: Blood α2,6-sialyltransferase activity increased and even surpassed the baseline for resting WT mice by week 8 in chimeras reconstituted with ST6GAL1-competent hematopoietic cells.
source: In contrast, blood accumulation of α2,6-sialyltransferase activity against Gal(β4)GlcNAc-o-Bn acceptor was dependent on re-establishment of ST6GAL1-competent hematopoietic cells, and increased and even surpassed the baseline for resting WT mice by week 8 (Figure 4c).

claim: Progenitor Lin-/c-kit+/Sca-1- (LK) and Lin-/c-kit+/Sca-1+ (LSK) populations, as well as CD41+ megakaryocyte lineage progenitors, were dramatically modified by cell non-autonomous extrinsic ST6GAL1.
source: Particularly, progenitor Lin-/c-kit+/Sca-1- (LK) and Lin-/c-kit+/Sca-1+ (LSK) populations, as well as CD41+ megakaryocyte lineage progenitors, were dramatically modified by cell non-autonomous extrinsic ST6GAL1, in comparison to CD11b+ myeloid cell subtypes and Ter119+ erythrocyte progenitors.

claim: Extracellular ST6GAL1 shows target-dependent bias towards CD11b-neg cells.
source: These obeservations demonstrate that hematopoietic-derived ST6GAL1 alters the sialylation of non-self cells, and further suggest target-dependent bias of the extracellular ST6GAL1 towards CD11b-neg cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential sialylation patterns observed in different cell types

claim: Hematopoietic cells alone, without contribution from the liver, were sufficient to maintain baseline blood ST6GAL1.
source: These data demonstrate that hematopoietic cells alone, without contribution from the liver the canonical source of circulating ST6GAL1, were sufficient not only to maintain baseline blood ST6GAL1, but also to confer cell surface SNA-reactivity onto other cells that were unable to express their own ST6GAL1.
evidence: Demonstrated through bone marrow transplantation experiments (Figure 4)

claim: Hematopoietic cells can confer cell surface SNA-reactivity onto other cells that are unable to express their own ST6GAL1.
source: These data demonstrate that hematopoietic cells alone, without contribution from the liver the canonical source of circulating ST6GAL1, were sufficient not only to maintain baseline blood ST6GAL1, but also to confer cell surface SNA-reactivity onto other cells that were unable to express their own ST6GAL1.
evidence: Demonstrated through bone marrow transplantation experiments (Figure 4)

claim: Almost all (roughly 75%) of the increase in blood ST6GAL1 activity can be attributed to B cells.
source: The data show that ST6GAL1 accumulated in the blood of the chimeras reconstituted with WT marrow, but not in in chimeras reconstituted with μMT marrow. Strikingly, almost all (roughly 75%) of the increase in blood ST6GAL1 activity could be attributed to B cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through comparison of bone marrow chimeras with and without B cells (Figure 4g)

claim: B cells directly express and release ST6GAL1 into the blood to restore extracellular levels in the absence of host ST6GAL1 expression.
source: Thus, the data demonstrate that B cells directly express and release ST6GAL1 into the blood to restore extracellular levels in the absence of host ST6GAL1 expression.

claim: Formalin-fixed and frozen whole femurs from chimeras where hematopoietic cells are the sole source of ST6GAL1 had strikingly patchy areas of SNA reactivity across the bone marrow.

claim: Uniform SNA reactivity was observed in chimeras where the recipients were ST6GAL1-competent.
source: In contrast, uniform SNAreactivity was observed in chimeras where the recipients were ST6GAL1-competent, for example μMT mice.

claim: The spatially punctate distribution of marrow α2,6-sialylation results only when hematopoietic cells are the sole source of ST6GAL1.

claim: The number of IgD+ B cells was modestly positively correlated with the SNA reactivity of bone marrow regions of interest.

claim: SNA+ cells in bone marrow were not limited to the IgD+ B cells, but often encompassed groups of cells in their vicinity.

claim: Some of the variation in bone marrow niche α2,6-sialylation can be attributed to the presence of mature IgD+ B cells.
source: Collectively, this suggests that some of the variation in bone marrow niche α2,6-sialylation can be attributed to the presence of mature IgD+ B cells.

claim: Plasma cells can remain for years within the bone marrow to maintain systemic titers of protective antibodies.
source: In contrast, plasma cells can remain for years within the bone marrow to maintain systemic titers of protective antibodies, and are thought to occupy a specialized niche in proximity to megakaryocytes, eosinophils, and soluble pro-survival factors (Wilmore and Allman, 2017).

claim: Plasma cells are thought to occupy a specialized niche in proximity to megakaryocytes, eosinophils, and soluble pro-survival factors.
source: In contrast, plasma cells can remain for years within the bone marrow to maintain systemic titers of protective antibodies, and are thought to occupy a specialized niche in proximity to megakaryocytes, eosinophils, and soluble pro-survival factors (Wilmore and Allman, 2017).

claim: ST6GAL1 expression in multiple myeloma varied dramatically from patient to patient.
source: ST6GAL1 expression in MM varied dramatically from patient to patient.
evidence: Demonstrated through histological analysis of patient samples (Figure 6a)

claim: ST6GAL1 expression in tumor cells was not associated with altered patient survival.
source: The expression of ST6GAL1 in tumor cells was not associated with altered patient survival (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Demonstrated through survival analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a

claim: Plasma cell burden and abundance of segmented neutrophils varied completely independently (r2 = 0.001, p=0.88).
source: However, whereas the plasma cell burden and abundance of segmented neutrophils varied completely independently (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b, r2 = 0.001, p=0.88), we observed a striking relationship between plasma cell ST6GAL1 expression and segmented neutrophils.
evidence: Demonstrated through correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b

claim: There is a strong negative correlation between ST6GAL1 score and presence of segmented neutrophils (r2 = 0.42, p=0.0083).
source: When ST6GAL1 score was compared to the frequency of granulocyte lineage cells, as assessed by a trained clinical pathologist, we identified a strong negative correlation between ST6GAL1 score and presence of segmented neutrophils (r2 = 0.42, p=0.0083) (Figure 6b).
evidence: Demonstrated through correlation analysis shown in Figure 6b

claim: Patients with low ST6GAL1 scores (<100) had higher frequencies of mature neutrophils (22.32 ± 4.11%).
source: Patients with low ST6GAL1 scores (<100) had higher frequencies of mature neutrophils (22.32 ± 4.11%), whereas those with high ST6GAL1 scores (>100) had markedly lower frequency (9.1 ± 2.6%) (Figure 6b inset).
evidence: Demonstrated through stratified analysis shown in Figure 6b inset

claim: Patients with high ST6GAL1 scores (>100) had markedly lower frequency of mature neutrophils (9.1 ± 2.6%).
source: Patients with low ST6GAL1 scores (<100) had higher frequencies of mature neutrophils (22.32 ± 4.11%), whereas those with high ST6GAL1 scores (>100) had markedly lower frequency (9.1 ± 2.6%) (Figure 6b inset).

claim: During systemic inflammation, B cells vacate the bone marrow due to the release of TNF-α and downregulation of CXCL12.
source: During systemic inflammation, B cells vacate the bone marrow due to the release of TNF-α and downregulation of CXCL12, salvaging space in preparation for the emergency generation of granulocytes (Ueda et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: B cells vacate the bone marrow during systemic inflammation to salvage space in preparation for the emergency generation of granulocytes.

claim: The 'B-helper' subset of neutrophils (NBH) can prime marginal zone B cells for antibody production during inflammation by the release of BAFF.
source: The newly-defined 'B-helper' subset of neutrophils (NBH) can prime marginal zone B cells for antibody production during inflammation by the release of BAFF (Scapini et al., 2003; Puga et al., 2012).

claim: B cells inhibit neutrophil functions including blocking chemotaxis and initiating β2 integrin-mediated apoptosis.

claim: B cell suppression of neutrophilic influx into the liver and spleen is necessary for the resolution of infections with intracellular organisms.
source: B cell suppression of neutrophilic influx into the liver and spleen is necessary for the resolution of infections with a number of intracellular organisms, where neutrophils can cause damaging local and systemic inflammation (Bosio and Elkins, 2001; Smelt et al., 2000; Buendía et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: Upregulation of serum ST6GAL1 during inflammation was attributed to the induction of hepatic expression.
source: Upregulation of serum ST6GAL1 during inflammation was attributed to the induction of hepatic expression, leading to the designation of ST6GAL1 as an acute phase reactant (Kaplan et al., 1983; Jamieson et al., 1993; Jamieson et al., 1987; Jamieson, 1988; van Dijk et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: ST6GAL1 has been designated as an acute phase reactant.

evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: B cells utilize multiple tissue-specific transcripts of ST6GAL1 during development.
source: However, it was also recognized that in addition to hepatocytes, B cells are sophisticated expressers of ST6GAL1, utilizing multiple tissue-specific transcripts during development (Wuensch et al., 2000; Wang et al., 1993; Lo and Lau, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature

claim: The limited endogenous expression of ST6GAL1 in hematopoietic stem and progenitor populations may be compensated for by secreted, extracellular enzyme.
source: Indeed, the limited endogenous expression of ST6GAL1 in hematopoietic stem and progenitor populations may be compensated for by secreted, extracellular enzyme, making the bone marrow microenvironment a distinct niche space for extrinsic sialylation (Nasirikenari et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns of sialylation and ST6GAL1 expression

claim: The bone marrow microenvironment is a distinct niche space for extrinsic sialylation.

claim: Hematopoietic cells were capable of independently reconstituting blood levels of ST6GAL1 in St6gal1KO mice to baseline WT levels over 8 weeks.
source: In our experiments, hematopoietic cells were capable of independently reconstituting blood levels of ST6GAL1 in St6gal1KO mice to baseline WT levels over 8 weeks, and the vast majority of this could be attributed to ST6GAL1 expression within B cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through bone marrow transplantation experiments (Figure 4g)

claim: The 50 kDa form of ST6GAL1 released by B cells appeared to be catalytically active.
source: The 50 kDa form, which appeared to be catalytically active, was the predominant ST6GAL1 form released by the BACE1-negative MM1.S cells.
evidence: Demonstrated through enzymatic activity assays (Figure 1d)

claim: The 50 kDa form of ST6GAL1 is consistent with an intact transmembrane domain.
source: While the nature and mechanism of release of the 50kDa ST6GAL1 form remain to be investigated, its size is consistent with an intact transmembrane domain, raising the possibility of the release of ST6GAL1 associated vesicles.
evidence: This is an inference based on the molecular weight of the observed form

claim: The 50 kDa form of ST6GAL1 raises the possibility of the release of ST6GAL1 associated vesicles.

claim: ST6GAL1 associated vesicles may facilitate shuttling of enzyme between specific cell types to mediate extrinsic sialylation.
source: If true, this mechanism may facilitate shuttling of enzyme between specific cell types to mediate extrinsic sialylation (McLellan, 2009; Zech et al., 2012).

claim: The 50 kDa form could represent a form of ST6GAL1 processed by signal peptide peptidases.
source: Alternately, the 50 kDa form could represent a form of ST6GAL1 processed by signal peptide peptidases, as reported for other glycosyltransferases, solubilizing the enzyme without significantly reducing its molecular weight (Voss et al., 2014; Kuhn et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism, supported by citations to prior literature

source: The sialylation of IgG by ST6GAL1 is necessary for the anti-inflammatory effects of IVIG therapy in autoimmune disease, and variations in serum IgG sialylation have been widely associated with inflammatory diseases (Pagan et al., 2018; Nimmerjahn and Ravetch, 2008; Biermann et al., 2016).

claim: Early studies documented concurrent increases in serum protein sialylation and sialyltransferase activity during malignancy, including in multiple myeloma.
source: Numerous early studies in both rodent models and humans have also documented concurrent increases in serum protein sialylation and sialyltransferase activity during malignancy, including in multiple myeloma, implying that ST6GAL1 expressing tumor cells are capable of secreting enzyme into the extracellular pool (Bernacki and Kim, 1977; Cohen et al., 1989b; Cohen et al., 1993; Chelibonova-Lorer et al., 1986; Dairaku et al., 1983; Gessner et al., 1993; Poon et al., 2005).

claim: Localized gradients of cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors create functional and developmental marrow niche spaces.
source: While localized gradients of cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors are already understood to create functional and developmental marrow niche spaces (Birbrair and Frenette, 2016), our data now underscore a novel role for extracellular glycan-modifying enzymes such as ST6GAL1 in the marrow hematopoietic environment.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature

claim: Extracellular glycan-modifying enzymes such as ST6GAL1 play a novel role in the marrow hematopoietic environment.

evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the study

claim: Extrinsic ST6GAL1 may have a broad ability to coordinate the development and function of multiple immune cell types.

evidence: Supported by citations to prior work by the authors

claim: Tumor-derived ST6GAL1 may dysregulate the development of bystander immune cells in the tumor microenvironment.
source: The strong negative association between human multiple myeloma ST6GAL1 expression and neutrophil prevalence indicates that tumor-derived ST6GAL1 may dysregulate the development of bystander immune cells in the tumor microenvironment, with a variety of potential implications.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed negative correlation in patient samples

claim: Biologic effects of ST6GAL1 in cancer extend beyond the cell-intrinsic modulation of oncogenic signaling pathways.
source: Collectively, our data hint at biologic effects of ST6GAL1 in cancer that extend beyond the cell-intrinsic modulation of oncogenic signaling pathways, instead being mediated by a novel, extrinsic axis of glycosylation, and galvanized by the growing importance of immune cells in malignancy.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data presented in the study
